items.content:
Everyone defending Jensen is trying to make it about the sex.

It’s not about the sex. 

It’s about how he enabled and even lobbied for Chinese AI, about how he subverted US policy, and how he carelessly left himself vulnerable to both blackmail and espionage.  

And it’s about how he utterly blew off the problems inherent appearance of conflict of interest, to the peril of his company, his country, and his industry.

He also left Nvidia open to endless litigation and investigation (which is why they may be forced to fire him despite his immense talents).

The fact that he also slept with an employee is just icing on the cake, in a way that further emphasizes his poor judgment, and that would only make the shareholder lawsuits worse.

Firing him will be a huge blow, but keeping him on is no longer tenable, either.

items.title: We're open-sourcing our latest versions of Decision Models: Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, and...
items.content:
We're open-sourcing our latest versions of Decision Models: Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, and making them free on @OpenRouter for a week.

The new capability in v1.3 models is "locate". This lets you describe what to find, and the model returns the matching text with character offsets. 

This is useful for batch-mode decision + evidence/entity extraction. On 17 out-of-domain NER, PII and extractive QA tasks, Decider models significantly outperform the best general extraction model.

And, on 63 of our own production classification tasks, v1.3 is 6.54 points more accurate than the classifiers we run today. 

Weights are open on Hugging Face: https://t.co/6olEOrOq4y

Weights are open on Hugging Face.

items.title:
Today we’re introducing ParseBench-2 - our most ambitious document parsing benchmark to date.

It is...
items.content:
Today we’re introducing ParseBench-2 - our most ambitious document parsing benchmark to date.

It is the only benchmark that provides both extreme granularity into every single type of production parsing error, while also making sure that metric scores are highly aligned with human judgment. We do this by painstakingly assigning severity scores to 330+ error types, and tuning each metric to match the severity scores. 
Existing benchmarks either use brittle deterministic metrics (e.g. OmniDocBench) or LLM-as-a-judge (ParseArena), which can help recognize equivalent representations but are coarse/stochastic/subject to bias by the prompt+model.

ParseBench-2 also contains:
✅ 4.3k+ document pages (double from ParseBench-1).
✅ An extra dimension (forms)
✅ Much better ground-truth across all dimensions compared to ParseBench-1.

This is the next evolution of ParseBench, our hugely popular benchmark that has 50k+ monthly downloads, over 150+ OCR solutions benchmarked, and has been adopted by companies like NVIDIA, Cohere, Aleph Alpha, Perplexity, and others.

Alongside ParseBench-2, we are also releasing OCRia-1.5 - a new family of document parsing models that powers all our modes in LlamaParse. They represent a massive step up in capabilities from our latest release, and are state of the art in parsing complex tables, forms, charts, formatting, and assigning bounding boxes to complex layouts.

Come check out our blog post, technical report, and website.

Blog: https://t.co/TKbfCyTjht
Technical Report: https://t.co/eAu0s6ttA1
Website: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX

If you’re interested in trying out our OCRia-1.5 capabilities, come sign up for LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8

🎉 Day-0 support for @thinkymachines’ Inkling-2-Small in vLLM!

A 500B MoE with text + image inputs a...
items.content:
🎉 Day-0 support for @thinkymachines’ Inkling-2-Small in vLLM!

A 500B MoE with text + image inputs and text output. Bring the image into the conversation: ask a question with visual context, and get a text response from the same model.

Under the hood: a new ViT image encoder, mixed NVFP4/MXFP8 MoE layers, and DSpark speculative decoding.

@inferact leads the vLLM integration and optimization, working with Thinking Machines Lab on model code and checkpoints. The work spans MoE and attention kernels, the vision encoder and image preprocessing, plus draft-model GEMMs for speculative decoding.

Thanks to the TML, Inferact and vLLM teams bringing the model to an open inference stack!

items.title:
Sad but still bullish on @nvidia!

I’m seeing a lot of people criticizing its structure and the lack...
items.content:
Sad but still bullish on @nvidia!

I’m seeing a lot of people criticizing its structure and the lack of a clear CEO successor. Having seen it from up close, I think a lot of this criticism is ill-informed and overly simplistic (as often happens when a company is run differently from the norm).

Obviously, important to remember that this structure made NV as successful as it is and powered the AI revolution. But beyond its past success, I think it’s also what makes the company antifragile for the future.

In my opinion, NV's distributed leadership and comfort with chaos are much more of a strength than a weakness, even without Jensen. They give an unusual number of leaders room to step up and keep the whole machine moving (as we've seen in the past few days). They also keep the company flexible enough to adapt to the next paradigms (open-source/local/agents/robots/biology/chemistry/...). They also encourage hard-working, self-motivated team members with a strong sense of belonging and a willingness to help each other which will matter a lot. 

Personally, with the right CEO (and NVIDIA has plenty of exceptional leaders internally who could take on that role), I believe NV can keep thriving and empower every company to become an AI company and every builder to become an AI builder.

To the @nvidia team: sending you strength and support, from me, the @huggingface team and so many people across the AI community. We need you and we’re rooting for you to carry @JensenHuang's mission forward! Taking care of his company, your company, is probably the best way to honor his legendary legacy! 

💚💚💚

items.content:
Vercel AI Product Lead @hp_arora warns that Jensen Huang's resignation is a major setback for US open-weight AI, as China continues to dominate frontier open-weight model releases:

"Jensen was a major voice for the open-weight models in the US as well as internationally."

"There's a lot that we don't know about that happened at NVIDIA, so obviously we can’t speculate there. But it is a setback."

"Open weight models were gaining a lot of share, and they're still in use with enterprises, but we haven't seen the same level of acceleration and model quality the way we were seeing before. Most of the frontier open-weight models are coming out of China."

"The optimist in me wants to believe that the world will be diverse in terms of the choice that developers have and customers have with the types of models they work on."
@vercel

items.title: In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from examples in its prompt without updating ...
items.content:
In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from examples in its prompt without updating its parameters. The article asks how this works in a specific, practical case: classifying sentences using arbitrary labels, such as assigning “foo” to positive examples and “bar” to negative ones. Earlier research had identified possible components but not how they combine into a working process. The article’s central finding is that, in the models tested, this form of learning is a gated lookup of information stored within the prompt—not an observable process of fitting a rule or updating model weights.

The authors traced this process in three base language models with 3–4 billion parameters. They used controlled pairs of prompts that differed in one sentence, label, or query, then intervened on model activations and attention heads to test which components carried each change. They compared selected components with random controls and repeated key tests on fresh prompts. They also tested other model sizes, an instruction-tuned model, and a small transformer trained from scratch.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/Dqa00NoTPl

items.title: Training language models through reinforcement learning can be expensive because each training examp...
items.content:
Training language models through reinforcement learning can be expensive because each training example may require very different computing effort. In particular, processing long generated responses costs more than processing short ones. The article addresses how to reach a target level of model performance at lower total computational cost, rather than simply reducing the number of training steps.

The article develops a general sampling method, Cost-Aware SGD, and tests an adaptation for language-model policy optimization called Cost-Aware GRPO. The method gives more weight to examples that are informative for updating the model, while accounting for how expensive they are to process. In experiments, response length represents cost, and the absolute value of each response’s advantage—a measure of its training signal—is used as a practical estimate of how informative it is. The authors provide mathematical analyses for finite-sum optimization, test the method in synthetic experiments, and evaluate it with 1.5-billion-, 4-billion-, and 8-billion-parameter models trained on mathematical reasoning tasks.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/eH5ywz4X7s

items.title: We reworked the MoE, attention, GEMM, mHC and indexer kernels for Rubin: bandwidth-bound data stays ...
items.content:
We reworked the MoE, attention, GEMM, mHC and indexer kernels for Rubin: bandwidth-bound data stays in each SM's own memory domain, SM107's wider MMA instructions do more work per issue. DEP2 prefill steps are about 28% faster, and DEP decode steps about 25% faster.

We also ported our specialized decode path to Rubin and rebuilt most of it for SM107. A step there is a chain of small kernels near their latency floor, so the wins are the gaps: all-reduces fused into the kernels behind them, the shared expert inside the routed GEMMs, and loads that start before the wait.

2/4

items.title: AI agents powered by LLMs are increasingly used to automate software engineering tasks, such as diag...
items.content:
AI agents powered by LLMs are increasingly used to automate software engineering tasks, such as diagnosing and fixing bugs across large codebases. A critical initial bottleneck in this workflow is code localization: accurately pinpointing the specific files and code entities that require modification. Existing automated tools approach every software issue from scratch with no prior knowledge of the codebase. By contrast, experienced human engineers rely on accumulated memory of past changes, recurring bug patterns, and knowledge of frequently modified modules. The article addresses this gap by investigating how agents can build and leverage long-term memory derived from a repository's version control history to improve localization accuracy.

The primary objective of the article is to design, implement, and evaluate RepoMem, an architecture that augments existing agentic frameworks with repository-level memory. Specifically, the article demonstrates how tapping into historical commits and module summaries improves the state-of-the-art localization tool, LocAgent, across standard industry benchmarks.

items.title: Diffusion language models generate answers through a sequence of partial drafts, revealing several t...
items.content:
Diffusion language models generate answers through a sequence of partial drafts, revealing several tokens at a time rather than writing strictly from left to right. This can make generation faster, but it complicates reinforcement-learning training: the probability of a finished answer is difficult to calculate exactly, and methods that reward the answer as a whole may fail to distinguish which intermediate decisions helped or hurt. The article addresses how to give those individual steps more informative training signals.

The article introduces PACT, a method that learns both the language model’s response policy and a score for each unfinished answer. The score estimates the promise of that partial answer and is anchored to the reward of the completed response. During training, PACT encourages each generation step’s change in preference relative to the original model to match the change in the partial answer’s score. This avoids estimating the probability of the full answer across all possible generation paths. The authors tested PACT by fine-tuning LLaDA-8B-Instruct on four reasoning tasks—grade-school arithmetic, competition mathematics, Countdown puzzles, and 4×4 Sudoku—and comparing it with the base model and existing post-training methods. The main comparison used the same number of training batches as a key baseline, though PACT’s batches took somewhat longer to run.

items.title: Rubin computes fast enough that a rack serves far more sessions at once, and their live prefixes out...
items.content:
Rubin computes fast enough that a rack serves far more sessions at once, and their live prefixes outgrow any per-rank cache, so we pooled the rack’s memory: one Mooncake KV pool across the DRAM and spare HBM of every tray, and the Engram tables sharded across GPU HBM and read over NVLink. Even at very high concurrency the hit rate stays at 96.5–97%, close to the theoretical maximum.

With no session pinned to a rank, Dynamo’s router sends each request to the least-loaded one: TTFT P90 drops from 0.98 s to 0.38 s.

3/4

items.content:
This is probably the best tool I've seen so far for developers building Python agents.

CanyonOS is open-source. It's free. It runs right on your computer.

When you run it on your codebase, you'll get all of the following:

1. It creates separate Docker containers to run your agents as separate services and handles communication between them.

2. It scales each agent independently. When one agent gets overloaded, it adds workers for that agent.

3. It traces requests across agents and model calls, including parallel branches.

4. It shows model usage and estimated model costs by agent and request.

5. It deploys your workflow behind a REST API, with asynchronous execution and a dashboard to inspect what happens.

The best part is that you don't need to change your code to use this!

Here is a link to the platform: https://t.co/H0HeVMqrVX

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

Turba Labs co-founder @HJWSchmidtke predicts that starting next year, the AI industry will have more chips than it has electricity to power them:

"It starts with the eyes. It's like having analytics, understanding what's actually going on down to what we call flow level."

"Every bits and pieces where it's landing, where it's being stored can lead to additional waste."

"Starting next year there will be a lot more chips available than there will be power available, so now you need to make the most out of the chips with existing power constraints."
@TurbaLabs

items.title: Many professionals rely heavily on feature-rich productivity tools like Microsoft Excel but routinel...
items.content:
Many professionals rely heavily on feature-rich productivity tools like Microsoft Excel but routinely utilize only a narrow set of basic functionalities, often depending on repetitive, error-prone manual operations. While existing AI assistants can provide help, they operate primarily on explicit text queries, placing the burden on users to formulate precise prompts and recognize their own inefficiencies. The article presents and evaluates InvisibleMentor, a system introducing vision-grounded task reflection that automatically infers completed actions directly from video screen recordings—without requiring backend application programming interfaces, event logs, or user prompting—to recommend superior, automated workflows.

The system utilizes a two-stage AI architecture. First, a vision-language model samples screen frames every five seconds to reconstruct spreadsheet states and sequential user actions. Second, a LLM analyzes this reconstructed workflow immediately after task completion to identify inefficiencies and produce structured, step-by-step alternative recommendations. The authors validated the system through a technical benchmark consisting of 25 recorded Excel sessions encompassing 14 routine spreadsheet actions, followed by a within-subjects laboratory study involving 20 spreadsheet users comparing InvisibleMentor against a prompt-based baseline, Excel Copilot.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/6jqvPcZiPV

@awiltschko I'm out of my zone of expertise, but I also think a naive view is sometimes helpful.

It...
items.content:
@awiltschko I'm out of my zone of expertise, but I also think a naive view is sometimes helpful.

It seems like you're describing some combination of bureaucracy and physical limits.

On physical limits, there are some of course, but my overall view on seeing a few biotech startups is that humans make many many mistakes, with experiments, data, theories, etc. When I say "generally smart", I imagine "almost always right". So if you imagine every human decision and make it correct, efficient and fast. Can our funnel for dish -> mouse -> human be much better? We only need a few wins.

On bureaucracy, America is incredibly capitalistic, if it becomes clear that the models are "just right", regulatory hurdles will start to clear. I think GLP-1s are already an example of this in that if something works, general competitive and capitalistic forces will cause it to accelerate.

A really cool part of this work is how we approach automated metric design.

Instead of crafting them by hand, we fully acknowledge coding agents are now often better at doing that.

What's important for us human to do, is to state our preference and have a scalable method to encode that.

This is how we made ParseBench-2 much more granular, robust, and aligned.

items.title: Small language models can gain reasoning ability from stronger models through on-policy distillation...
items.content:
Small language models can gain reasoning ability from stronger models through on-policy distillation: the student generates its own responses and receives feedback from a teacher. But standard methods apply that feedback equally across generated tokens, even though most signals add little information and a small number of extreme negative signals can dominate training. The resulting updates can suppress useful reasoning paths, reduce response diversity, and sometimes leave the student worse than it started. The article examines whether allocating teacher feedback more selectively can make this transfer more stable and efficient.

The article introduces REOPOLD, a method that adjusts which teacher signals affect training, how strongly negative signals count, and how these rules change over time. The authors tested it on mathematical, visual, and tool-using reasoning tasks, comparing compact students trained with REOPOLD against standard distillation and other baselines. Their evaluations included multiple model sizes, teacher–student pairings, benchmark sets, and a visual self-distillation setting. In their analysis of standard training, the most negative one percent of token-level signals accounted for more than 95 percent of estimated update energy early in training, while the student quickly reduced support for responses it could produce before training.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/FBhh9VKtcM

items.summary: Burkov summarizes a research paper introducing REOPOLD, a method for on-policy distillation that selectively allocates teacher feedback across tokens and reshapes how negative signals are weighted over time, improving stability and efficiency when training small student models on math, visual, and tool-use reasoning tasks.

But standard methods apply that feedback equally across generated tokens, even though most signals add little information and a small number of extreme negative signals can dominate training. The resulting updates can suppress useful reasoning paths, reduce response diversity, and sometimes leave the student worse than it started. The article examines whether allocating teacher feedback more selectively can make this transfer more stable and efficient.

The article introduces REOPOLD, a method that adjusts which teacher signals affect training, how strongly negative signals count, and how these rules change over time. The authors tested it on mathematical, visual, and tool-using reasoning tasks, comparing compact students trained with REOPOLD against standard distillation and other baselines. Their evaluations included multiple model sizes, teacher–student pairings, benchmark sets, and a visual self-distillation setting. In their analysis of standard training, the most negative one percent of token-level signals accounted for more than 95 percent of estimated update energy early in training, while the student quickly reduced support for responses it could produce before training.

items.title: Google's new Gemini 4 Hydrogen has Intelligence just below Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, at a t...
items.content:
Google's new Gemini 4 Hydrogen has Intelligence just below Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, at a third of Sonnet’s cost but ~2.5x that of GPT-6.1 Sol

@GoogleDeepMind has released their third new model in six weeks. Gemini 4 Hydrogen introduces an xhigh reasoning level and scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, with strengths in visual reasoning and non-hallucination. This places it 1 point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), at ~32% of Sonnet’s cost but ~2.5x that of GPT-6.1 Sol. With high reasoning, Gemini 4 Hydrogen matches the Intelligence of Gemini 4 Argon for ~19% of the Cost per Task

Key takeaways:

➤ The new xhigh reasoning level scores 54 on the Intelligence Index: xhigh is the first reasoning level above high on a Gemini model, and puts Hydrogen 1 point below Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), and 4 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (high). With default (high) reasoning, Gemini 4 Hydrogen scores 51, just behind GPT-6.1 Sol (xhigh, 52) and Claude Opus 5.5 (high, 52)

➤ Strong visual reasoning, presentation and non-hallucination: On GDP.pdf, a visual reasoning benchmark over long documents, it scores 33% all-pass on medium reasoning, the tied #1 score on the benchmark. On AA-Omniscience, Hydrogen has one of the lowest hallucination rates recorded at 8%, compared with 43% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and 52% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). On AA-Briefcase, our agentic knowledge work evaluation, graders rate Hydrogen's presentation above other Gemini models, including Carbon

➤ Weaker on agentic terminal work: Hydrogen scores 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 50% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, covering agentic coding and scientific research workflows in the terminal. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) scores 64% and 53%, and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) scores 56% and 58%. xhigh reasoning helps on the science tasks, lifting Terminal-Bench-Science from 41% at high to 50%, but makes no difference on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (54% at both). Science scores are even across domains, from 46% in earth sciences to 53% in physical sciences

➤ Low cost for its intelligence, with high token use at xhigh: Hydrogen is priced at $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens. At xhigh it costs ~32% as much per task as Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) for near-equal intelligence, but ~2.5x as much as GPT-6.1 Sol (max). xhigh nearly doubles output tokens compared with high for a 3 point gain in Intelligence, and Cost per Task falls from $3.16 at xhigh to $1.87 at high. Medium ($0.80) and low ($0.29) cost less again, but score 41 and 27 on the Intelligence Index

➤ On the Time per Task vs. Intelligence Pareto frontier: Gemini 4 Hydrogen has an output speed of ~200 output tokens per second. With high, medium, and low reasoning effort, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is on the Time per Task vs. Intelligence Pareto frontier, meaning no models are both more intelligent and have a lower Time per Task

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Reasoning efforts: Gemini 4 Hydrogen offers four reasoning levels (low, medium, high, and xhigh) with xhigh new in this release

➤ Pricing: $1.50/$7.50 per 1M input/output tokens. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.075)

Congratulations to the @GoogleDeepMind team on the launch!
